Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We bring the Minster of Water and Sanitation to fly in a helicopter over the shores of the Vaal Dam where raw sewage from all the towns around the dam threatens Gauteng's water supply

Summary:
In June we broke the story of how Deneysville's sewage treatment plant was over-capacity and how raw sewage was flooding into the Vaal Dam. For months the residents kept on sending us a steady supply of damning photographs and videos of how the problem was being ignored. Now it seems a fence has been erected around one of the pump stations -- but not much more and untreated effluent still reaches the dam. Meanwhile we have collected similar damning evidence of gross pollution from towns further upstream, from Oranjeville, to Standerton, to Secunda, to Villiers where export grain silos have been contaminated by e.coli -- a sure sign of sewage pollution. We take the Minister to survey the damage and tell us how she is planning to fix these problems.

Press Release:


Foul Dam Water 2
In June this year Carte Blanche exposed the shocking extent to which failed sewerage systems surrounding the Vaal catchment area are polluting this vital water supply. New evidence now reveals that multiple municipalities are knowingly pumping sewage directly into the Vaal or allowing pollution of the dam through sheer neglect. Carte Blanche shows government our findings and asks for answers as to what will be done about this ticking water quality time bomb?

PROMOS:

Ten second
VO: Progress in Deneysville after Carte Blanche’s expose – is there hope on the horizon for the sewage polluted Vaal Dam, a water source for millions?

Fifteen second
DG MARGARET-ANN DIEDERICHS: I hope Derek that as you went back to Deneysville and to other areas where you’ve seen that there’s been progress, that in the months to come you will also see that there is progress in the upper Vaal.
VO: Help is on the way for the Vaal Dam – but can it be sustained?

Fifteen second
VO: Sewage treatment problems from Deneysville to Villiers…but are there signs of a turnaround?
DG MARGARET-ANN DIEDERICHS: I can indicate what the timeframes will be and I can indicate what the priority areas will be and for those, we will certainly allocate funding.

Script:


FOUL DAM WATER 2
The holiday town of Deneysville on the banks of the Vaal Dam has in recent months become a hotbed of activism around rising levels of pollution from the town’s limping sewage system.
DEREK LINK: Late in June we exposed the lack of sanitation in Deneysville, raw sewage floating in the streets, a treatment plant in disarray, and millions being spent on a pipeline that was of absolutely no use.
The plant built for about 4000 people was servicing 20,000. In any sewage system, what comes in should be processed, and similar quantities of acceptably treated effluent released back into the environment – in the case of Deneysville, the Vaal Dam. But the small portion of waste reaching the works was being inadequately treated and pumped in an old pipeline to the Dam, while much sewage wasn’t even reaching the plant. The municipality built a new pipeline, but the national department of water and sanitation sent them back to the drawing board to properly apply for a water use license.
PEET SCHABORT: Another thing with this pipeline – as quickly as they lay it, they covered it. In other words, the stones that were dug up were piled on top and in time they will push through the pipe.
IRENE MAIN: In untreated sewage you get two pests – one is cryptosporidium and the other is giardia. Rand Water actually advised us they were picking up these two pests in their filtration process…while they can treat this, it’s expensive to treat. And at the end of the day the cost is going to be passed on to the consumer.
KATHY MANTEN: It’s our drinking water for the rest of the country – or for Gauteng at least and if it’s polluted it’s such a huge body of water – to try and correct that will be a nightmare.
DR SHAN HOLMES: These practices are in fact a clear-cut case of water pollution that is in fact criminally libellous. You’re looking at a potential of cholera, typhus, salmonella outbreaks. This has an immediate and is a major risk for public health.
At the time, the municipality’s spokesman denied the charge of pollution.
GINO ALBERTS: Those are claims…allegations.
After our broadcast the Deneysville activists kept relentless pressure on authorities by recording evidence of every spill and breakdown.
The dam holds drinking water for 12-million people in Gauteng. From here it is abstracted and purified by the utility Randwater. Their quarterly reports on the final effluent from treatment plants along the Vaal’s shores, show rising e.coli contamination.
Carte Blanche undertook a research roadtrip to investigate sanitation conditions further along the Vaal.
In STANDERTON pump stations were blocked up and flooded. Sewage was streaming across a main road into the Vaal River. Fixing the pump stations didn’t seem impossible, as civil society activists Afriforum was facilitating a clean-up with funds from provincial Water and Sanitation and the municipality’s cooperation. Afriforum’s own funds paid for a pipe to reconnect parts of the system.
At ORANJEVILLE, unprocessed waste was flowing out of the pipes into the dam.
VILLIERS was an eye-opener. A town of about twenty thousand people, with flooded pump stations near silos that house export grain. The treatment works were standing still…although construction was underway to expand the plant – and a dose of chlorine had just been added to the final treatment stage form where water is piped to the Vaal river.
While municipalities are responsible for sewage treatment, the national government is the custodian of water resources like the Vaal Dam and River, so we invited Minister of Water and Sanitation Nomvula Mokonyane to join us on a fly-over fact-finding mission. The Minister made – and postponed – two appointments – but with all arrangements in place, we had to leave without her.
Our pilot, Menno Parsons is a businessman who volunteers his helicopter for environmental activists Bateleurs.
DEREK WATTS: Menno, your first flight for Bateleurs.
MENNO PARSONS: I was supposed to do it for the rhinos about two weekends ago in the Kruger Park and I was excited about this wildlife thing and flying for the environment and you gave me something different.
DEREK WATTS: Gave you the sewerage farms.
MENNO PARSONS: The sewerage farms ya, but still for the environment and really exciting to be a part of it you know.
The Bateleurs gives a free service to researchers and media that work for the environment – pilots and aircraft owners volunteer their resources to provide an aerial perspective on the use and abuse of earth’s resources. Menno set us down next to the silos where we met retired grain trader and now local opposition councillor Pieter van der Westhuizen.
PIETER VAN DER WESTHUIZEN: I started this battle in 2009 when I eventually discovered that the pump at that mini-pump station got stolen in November 2009, so since then…years of consistent begging, battles…
Recently Pieter witnessed how a load of soya beans, found to be contaminated with e.coli had to be dug out of the pits – an event that if it became a trend, could destroy agricultural exports.
DEREK WATTS: This water is flowing is flowing directly from the so-called final treatment plant – I hesitate to call it water because you saw how contaminated it was and it’s flowing directly into the Vaal river…just a few hundred metres from the drinking water purification plant.
Villiers and the town of Frankfort fall under the Mafube municipality where four high court orders over ten years have been obtained, compelling the Municipal Manager to fix infrastructure and prevent spillages.
PIETER VAN DER WESTHUIZEN: There are court orders to the effect that the municipal manager should be jailed for 90 days because he actually is in contempt of the court order which stipulated that the spillage of sewerage at Frankfort should be dealt with.
The Dept of Water and Sanitation have long diagnosed under-investment in infrastructure as the cause of poor sanitation in their Green Drop Reports. So have the National Planning Commission and even Human rights Commission.
In Deneysville we were greeted with better news. Kathy Manten whose family owns the local marina says the community and media pressure has led to some activity.
KATHY MANTEN: I’m really happy and pleased that they are making some improvements, making some efforts to rehabilitate this sewerage works and hopefully it will work properly.
This situation has turned retired surveyor Peet Schabort into a local sleuth and videographer.
16:37 (DW) Peet, do you feel that the work you’ve done as a community has paid off here?
16:45 (Peet) I think so. But of course with the media, I think people like you …I think that makes all the difference.
Irene Main form SAVE the Vaal Environment is far more guarded.
IRENE MAIN: I’d say at this stage things have improved yes, but overall we still have an issue with sewerage that is being diverted to a quarry which is a health hazard…it’s not fenced off; children can still go there. If they fall in they’re gonna drown and they’re gonna get sick.
DEREK WATTS: Well there’s still no gate, but this pump station is unrecognisable compared to our last visit – not a sign of raw sewage, the auger is turning, and it’s wonderful to see that at least there’s been some progress.
The Director General of Water and Sanitation Margaret-Ann Diederichs is the first permanent DG after four years of officials acting in the post. She is well familiar with the picture we painted for her in the different towns.
MARGARET-ANN DIEDRICKS: (looking at visuals of the different towns) It’s now common cause Derek that’s there been decades of under-investment and maintenance and operations. There are many and competing priorities. Of course it’s not just an issue of focusing on the Vaal – it is an area that we are certainly wanting to have pristine water there because it supplies water to a large number of sectors and communities. I can say that we will prioritise and we will incrementally work towards ensuring that the upper Vaal systems are dealt with and that the critical points are dealt with immediately.
DEREK WATTS: So you’re not promising miracles.
MARGARET-ANN DIEDRICKS: I can’t, not with the competing priorities that there are but what I can promise you is that there will be a plan and I can indicate what the timeframes will be and I can indicate what the priority areas will be and for those, we will certainly allocate funding.
Determining priorities finally brought the municipality and community of Deneysville into one room last week – working together on a funding proposal for the national department.
MARGARET-ANN DIEDRICKS: We are committed to ensure that we provide safe water and a dignified sanitation system to all – and I hope Derek, that in the ensuing months we will be able to make good on that and that as you went back to Deneysville and to other areas where you’ve seen that there’s been progress, that in the months to come you will also see that there is progress in the upper Vaal.
DEREK WATTS: Would you join us or would say the Minister join us in say, six months’ time, going back there early next year?
MARGARET-ANN DIEDRICKS: I can certainly commit myself to joining you, to taking you on that roadshow, to show the progress without a doubt – and I’m sure that Minister would have no problem in joining us as well.
